auspicious

/aw-SPISH-uss/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Auspicious means favorable; suggesting that success is likely to come — a promising sign, not present-tense joy.

The bakery's first morning felt auspicious: a line out the door before the ovens had even finished heating.

Example

The community garden's opening spring could not have started better. The last frost came two weeks early, the hardware store donated a truckload of topsoil unasked, and forty families signed up for twenty plots. "An auspicious beginning," the coordinator wrote in her log — not because anything had been harvested yet, but because every early sign pointed toward a thriving season ahead.

Nothing has actually succeeded yet — the word fits because the early frost date, free topsoil, and long waitlist are all signs pointing toward future success.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

promising: Promising means showing signs of future success, and it usually attaches to the thing with potential itself -- a promising student, a promising script. Auspicious attaches instead to the signs and circumstances around a beginning: the timing, the omens, the early turnout. The violinist is promising; her opening night is auspicious.

favorable: Favorable means working in your favor right now -- favorable terms, a favorable review, a favorable ruling all give you a present advantage. Auspicious is future-facing: it reads early signs as pointing toward success still to come. A favorable ruling helps you today; an auspicious start only predicts good things ahead.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

ill-omened: marked by signs of coming misfortune

bleak: offering little hope of success

Where it sits · how strongly the signs promise success

encouraging → auspicious → providential

encouraging vs. auspicious: Encouraging signs merely lift your hopes; auspicious signs point clearly toward a successful outcome ahead.

providential vs. auspicious: Providential is stronger than auspicious — good fortune so perfectly timed it seems arranged by fate itself.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — auspic: bird-watching for omens (Latin avis 'bird' + specere 'to look')

Suffix — -ious: characterized by

Put it together: Auspicious preserves an ancient Roman job: the auspex, or 'bird-watcher,' who read the future in the flight of birds before any major undertaking. The word fuses avis ('bird') with specere ('to look') — the root you know from inspect and perspective. When the birds flew the right way, the day was auspicious: the signs pointed to success.

Use the root in a new word: perspective: Your perspective is literally the way you look through at things — the same Latin root specere, 'to look,' that Roman bird-watchers used when declaring a day auspicious.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal, slightly literary; about beginnings and signs

Auspicious is future-facing: it describes signs and beginnings that point toward success, not happiness happening right now — an auspicious opening day can be a quiet one, and a joyful party can still be ill-omened.
